notes.meaning: The Lord speaks again to Zechariah to comfort His people after a long season of hardship. He declares that He has a burning love for Jerusalem and is deeply moved to protect His city. His fierce passion also means He will hold her cruel enemies accountable.

God promises that He will return to live among His people in Jerusalem. When His holy presence fills the city, Jerusalem will be known for loyalty and truth instead of wickedness. The temple hill will once again be called the holy mountain, set apart for the Lord.

Jerusalem will enjoy such lasting peace and safety that men and women will live to a very old age, resting along the streets with walking sticks. The town squares once emptied by war will be filled with boys and girls playing freely without fear. This pictures a secure and thriving community blessed by God.

The small group of returned exiles felt that such total peace and joy was too wonderful to ever come true. God asks them whether something that seems impossible to human beings could ever be impossible for Him. His power is far greater than human weakness or doubt.

The Lord promises to gather His scattered people from every direction, from the east to the west. He will bring them safely back to live in Jerusalem under His care. There He will renew His covenant promise, being their faithful God while they live as His devoted people.

The Lord encourages the builders to take heart and work hard, listening to the prophets who urged them to rebuild the temple. Before they began this work, life was miserable, with no profit from their labor, constant danger from enemies, and neighbors fighting one another. God had allowed these troubles to show them their need of Him.

God announces that He will no longer treat the surviving remnant with hardship as He did in the past. He promises peace and good crops, sending rain and dew so that the ground and vineyards produce rich harvests. He gives all these good things to His people as their lasting inheritance.

In earlier days, surrounding nations used the names of Judah and Israel as an example of a cursed people. Now God promises to rescue them completely so that their name will become an example of blessing. Because God is on their side, they do not need to be afraid and can work with strength.

God reminds the people that when their ancestors sinned, He firmly carried out the discipline He had decreed without changing His mind. In the same reliable way, He is now completely determined to do good to Jerusalem and Judah. Because God's promise to bless is just as certain, His people have no reason to be afraid.

God calls His people to live in a way that matches His blessings by speaking the truth and making fair decisions in their public courts. They must not plot secretly to harm their neighbors or make false promises under oath. God hates all such deceit because He is holy and loves justice.

The Lord answers the question about fasting by telling the people that four annual fasts marking the fall of Jerusalem will turn into cheerful feasts. Because God is restoring their city, their mourning will give way to celebrations of joy and gladness. In response, they must truly love honesty and peace.

God reveals that people from many different cities will encourage one another to travel together to seek the Lord. Whole nations and powerful rulers will come to Jerusalem to pray and ask for God's mercy. Instead of being ignored, the worship of the true God will attract people from all over the earth.

Zechariah pictures ten men from different nations and languages taking firm hold of the coat of one Jew. They will beg to go along with him to worship, because they have seen clearly that the living God is with His people. God's presence among His followers will draw the world to Himself.

differ.view: This points to a future earthly kingdom, where Jewish people will lead the nations of the world in seeking and worshiping God in Jerusalem.
This prophecy is fulfilled in the church, as people from all nations come to God through Jesus Christ, the Jewish Savior.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early church teachers saw the Jew in this verse as Christ Himself, with Gentiles taking hold of His robe by faith to receive salvation.
